Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Sex: Sex, Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Leilani, at nineteen, had always found solace and purpose on the water, the rhythmic pull of the nets a familiar comfort. But that changed one pre-dawn morning as she cycled towards the docks, the air still cool and quiet. Just ahead, a small child on a bicycle, barely visible in the dim light, was struck by a car that didn't stop. The sickening crunch of metal and plastic, followed by the screech of tires disappearing into the distance, was etched into her mind. She froze, unable to move, too far away to do anything but witness the horrific scene unfold. The child lay motionless, the bicycle a mangled mess. Leilani could only stand there, a desperate, paralysing helplessness washing over her, before the distant wail of sirens began to cut through the silence.

Since then, the world had become a minefield. The memory of the accident forced its way into her mind at unpredictable times, often when she was trying to focus on her work, mending nets or navigating the boat. Sometimes it would arrive as a full, vivid replay, the child’s small form, the twisted bicycle, the vanishing taillights. Other times, it was more abstract, a sudden, overwhelming wave of emotion – pure terror, grief, or that searing guilt – without any clear image attached. When she did remember the event, an intense, crushing guilt would flood her, the thought "I should have protected others and I failed" echoing relentlessly in her head.

Her body, too, seemed to have a mind of its own. Walking along the docks, the sound of footsteps behind or nearby would send a jolt of fear through her, her heart hammering before she even had time to consciously register a threat. It felt as if her body reacted to danger before she had even had time to think, a primal alarm system constantly misfiring. The sight of a bicycle, even one leaning innocently against a wall, or certain related sounds – the faint screech of tires, a distant car horn, even the specific clang of metal – would trigger an instant surge of adrenaline, making her scan her surroundings frantically, convinced something bad was happening again. She often felt a profound sense of betrayal by her own physiology, believing, "My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe."

Her concentration, once sharp and reliable for the demands of fishing, had plummeted. It was increasingly difficult to focus on tasks on the boat, her mind constantly drifting or hyper-vigilantly scanning the horizon for unseen threats. When something took longer than expected – a fishing line snagging, a boat engine sputtering, or her partner being a few minutes late – she would immediately assume something bad was happening, her imagination conjuring the worst possible scenarios.

To cope, Leilani had developed new habits. She began to overwork, volunteering for extra shifts, staying late to clean equipment, anything to keep her hands busy and her mind distracted from the intrusive thoughts that plagued her when she was alone. When she was off work, she spent long hours on her phone, playing games or scrolling the internet, using the digital world as a shield against her inner turmoil. This screen escape became her primary way to avoid thinking, a desperate attempt to drown out the noise in her head. Her relationship with her partner, once a source of comfort, became strained. The intimacy of sex felt overwhelming, a vulnerability she couldn't tolerate, so she began to avoid it, creating an emotional distance between them.

She also noticed a terrifying shift in her temperament. Small frustrations could ignite a sudden, intense rage within her, a feeling so overwhelming that she would sometimes fear, "I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible." This fear only added to her sense of being dangerous and out of control.

The constant exhaustion from overworking, the strain on her relationship, and the terrifying realization that she was losing control of her emotions finally brought Leilani to seek help. She felt trapped in a constant cycle of fear and guilt, desperately hoping to find a way to quiet the relentless alarms in her body and mind, and to stop believing that she was inherently flawed and dangerous.
